title: Tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon: where did that word go?
description: Why does a familiar word feel so close? Discover the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon, partial clues and why confidence can get ahead of recall.

sections.title: You can picture it. You cannot name it.
sections.html:
The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon is the feeling that you know a word but cannot quite bring it to mind. It feels frustratingly close.

You can picture a brass instrument and mime its sliding tube. You are convinced you know its name. “That musical thing” is doing a lot of work until trombone finally arrives.

sections.title: Some pieces can turn up first
sections.html:
In their 1966 experiment, Roger Brown and David McNeill read definitions of uncommon words to people. During some tip-of-the-tongue moments, participants could recall details such as letters or the number of syllables.

Brown later described the experiment himself. The whole word could be missing while parts of its shape were available. A clue, however, is not a guarantee.

sections.title: A confident clue can be wrong
sections.html:
A 2023 study by Huebert and colleagues adds a twist. When participants could freely report clues, they offered more partial information during tip-of-the-tongue states, without being more accurate among the responses they supplied.

In a first-letter guessing task, people could also feel sure they knew the letter while guessing incorrectly. That almost-knowing feeling deserves a little caution.

sections.title: The almost-answer is interesting too
sections.html:
A quiz answer can feel close long before you can say it. That gap between confidence and recall is part of what makes this ordinary mental pause so intriguing.

For another surprise, try picturing a familiar logo from memory, or explore why a doorway can interrupt a thought. Even everyday remembering has its plot twists.
